turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, doctor, it is... gosh, it is just so much all at once. But I guess what really brings me in, what finally made me pick up the phone and make the appointment, is that I feel like I am constantly running on a motor lately. I mean, just constantly, from the second I wake up. 

I am a special education teacher, and you know, that takes a lot of energy on a good day, but it is like I finish one thing at school—whether it is an evaluation meeting or getting the kids settled or sorting out the classroom materials—and I immediately jump right into the next thing. There is no pause. There is no taking a breath or having a cup of coffee. And you would think at 58 years old I would be slowing down a bit, maybe sitting in the staff room for five minutes between periods, but I just cannot do it. 

And it is the exact same way at home, it really is. I walk through the front door and I am immediately fixing a loose hinge in the garage, and then before I even put the tools away I am in the kitchen scrubbing the counters, and then I am out in the yard pulling weeds. I just jump from task to task to task without ever being able to shut myself off. It is like the off-switch is completely broken. My family tells me to just sit down and relax for ten minutes, but if I try to sit in the recliner in the evening, just to rest my bones, my whole body is just humming, pushing me to get back up and do something else. I just never, ever shut down.

turns.doctor_question: When you say you're constantly running on this motor, how many hours of sleep are you actually getting at night? And do you feel rested, or do you feel like you need less sleep than you used to?
turns.patient_response:
Sleep? Well, it is not that I feel like I *need* less sleep, if that makes sense. It is not like I am one of those people who can just sleep for three hours and wake up feeling like a million bucks. No, no, I am bone tired. I mean, you can imagine, chasing after middle schoolers with severe behavioral needs all day, and then doing yard work until the sun goes down... I am physically exhausted. My joints ache. 

But when I finally do try to get into bed—and getting into bed is a whole elaborate process, let me tell you, because I will go to brush my teeth and suddenly realize the bathroom sink needs scrubbing, and then before I know it I am organizing the entire medicine cabinet at 11:30 at night while my wife is just begging me to please turn off the light and come to bed—but when I finally do lay down, I don't feel rested at all. 

As for exactly how many hours I am actually getting, gosh, I don't even really know. I don't keep track of the exact numbers. I guess once I finally, truly crash and burn for the night, I probably sleep a normal amount? I am not really sure. But I definitely never wake up feeling refreshed or rejuvenated. I wake up and... boom, the motor is just running again. My feet hit the floor and I am instantly thinking about the IEP meetings I have that day, and whether I need to mow the lawn before it rains on Thursday, and I am just instantly off to the races again. So no, I definitely don't feel like I need less sleep, I honestly probably need a lot more! It is just that I cannot seem to make myself stop doing things long enough to actually get into the bed in the first place.

turns.doctor_question: During these times when you feel this motor running and you're jumping from task to task, do you ever experience sudden episodes where your heart races, you feel short of breath, or you have a sense of panic or dread—or is it more of a constant restless drive without those acute episodes?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, it's nothing like that. I don't get those... what did you call them, acute episodes? No, my heart isn't pounding out of my chest like I'm having a heart attack or something, and I don't feel like I can't breathe. It's not a panic thing. I don't feel dread, really. I mean, I might feel stressed about all the paperwork I have to do—because, let me tell you, the amount of paperwork they expect from special ed teachers these days is just astronomical, it's a mountain of forms for every single student, and if you miss one signature the whole district gets in an uproar—but it's not a sudden panic attack. 

It's really just exactly what you said, that constant restless drive. It's just this hum in my bones. Like yesterday, for example, I was trying to watch a movie with my wife—she loves those historical dramas, the ones that are three hours long and very slow-paced—and I was sitting there on the couch, and I wasn't panicked, I wasn't short of breath, but my leg was bouncing, and my fingers were drumming on the armrest, and all I could think about was the fact that the gutters really need cleaning before the autumn leaves start falling in earnest. And I kept trying to focus on the movie, but the physical urge to just get up and get the ladder out of the shed was so overwhelming. I ended up getting up and reorganizing the Tupperware drawer while watching from the kitchen doorway. So it's not fear or panic, it's just... I just have to be moving. I have to be doing something. It never spikes into terror, it just stays at this constant, exhausting level of 'go, go, go.'

turns.doctor_question: When you're experiencing this constant motor drive and restlessness, do you find yourself worrying a lot—like, is your mind racing with anxious thoughts about things that might go wrong, or is it more that your body just won't settle down while your mind might be relatively calm?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's... it's definitely not worry, not in the sense of being anxious about things going wrong. I'm not sitting there chewing my fingernails worrying that the house is going to burn down or that I'm going to lose my job or anything like that. It's not a fearful racing mind. I mean, sure, I have the normal stresses, like I mentioned with the paperwork, or worrying if one of my students is going to have a meltdown during an assembly, which, believe me, happens more often than you'd think and requires a whole protocol to handle. But that's just normal teacher stuff, you know? It's not this paralyzing, anxious worry.

My mind *is* racing, though, but it's racing with... with tasks. With things to do. It's like a running to-do list that just never ends and keeps scrolling and scrolling in my head. Like I said about the gutters, right? I wasn't *worried* the gutters were going to cause a flood and destroy the foundation of the house, I just couldn't stop thinking about the physical act of cleaning them. It's like my brain is a pinball machine, and the ball is just bouncing from "fix the hinge" to "grade the math worksheets" to "clean the Tupperware drawer" to "mow the lawn." 

So my mind isn't calm, exactly, because it's always plotting the next five things I need to physically do, but it's not anxious. It's just... driven. And my body is just following along, or maybe my body is driving the brain, I don't even know which comes first anymore! It's just this physical inability to settle. My wife will say, "Just turn your brain off for a minute," and I try to explain to her that it's not like I'm sitting there fretting over the state of the world, I'm just physically incapable of sitting still when my brain is telling me there are fourteen things in the garage that need organizing right this very second. So no, it's not anxious worry, it's just this overwhelming urge to be doing, doing, doing, all the time.

turns.doctor_question: Has your wife or anyone else ever noticed you stop breathing during the night, or gasp or choke in your sleep? Or do you ever wake up gasping for air?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, nothing like that. My wife—she's a remarkably light sleeper, bless her heart. I mean, if the neighbor's cat so much as walks across our front porch, she's sitting straight up in bed. So she would absolutely notice if I stopped breathing or started choking or gasping in the middle of the night. She's never mentioned anything of the sort. 

What she *does* mention, and honestly she brings it up at least twice a week, is how much I toss and turn. Because even when I'm asleep, I guess I'm still moving. I'm kicking the sheets, flipping over, adjusting the pillows... we actually had to upgrade to a king-size mattress about five years ago, because when we had the queen, I was practically knocking her off the edge with all my thrashing around. And even with the extra space, she still threatens to send me to the guest room down the hall sometimes just so she can get some peace! 

But as far as my breathing goes? No, perfectly normal. I never wake up gasping for air or feeling choked. Like I said before, when I wake up, I just wake up instantly wide awake and ready to go, thinking about lesson plans or whether I need to change the oil in the lawnmower. There's no choking or struggling to breathe at all, just a whole lot of restless kicking.

turns.doctor_question: During the day, do you find yourself feeling excessively drowsy or struggling to stay awake, even though you're constantly moving around and doing things? For example, do you ever nod off unintentionally during the day, like while driving or sitting at your desk?
turns.patient_response:
Drowsy? Oh, gosh, no. No, no, no. I'm the exact opposite of drowsy. If anything, I honestly wish I could feel a little drowsy sometimes just to get a break from the motor, you know? It might be nice to just sit in a chair and actually feel relaxed enough to let my eyes drift shut, but that just doesn't happen for me. 

I mean, if you think about my day... I'm a special ed teacher, so from the moment that first bell rings at 7:45 AM, I am on my feet. And even when I do have a prep period—which is supposed to be my 45 minutes of quiet time sitting at my desk grading or doing all that IEP paperwork I was telling you about—I'm absolutely not nodding off. I can't even sit in the chair properly! I'm usually pacing around the back of the classroom, or I'm standing up at the filing cabinet to read things, or I'm reorganizing the sensory bin for the third time that week. There's just no off switch. 

Sometimes the other teachers in the breakroom—like Susan, the art teacher, she's always complaining about the 2 PM slump and drinking her third cup of coffee, and she'll ask me how I have so much energy. I always have to laugh because it doesn't feel like *good* energy, it's just that my body literally cannot stop moving. 

And you mentioned driving—never. I have a 40-minute commute each way, taking the interstate, and I am wide awake the entire time. I'm usually listening to an audiobook or the news, drumming my fingers on the steering wheel, thinking about what I'm going to make for dinner or what repairs the house needs. I don't ever get that heavy-eyelid feeling, not even a little bit. It's like my body doesn't know how to power down until I literally exhaust myself late at night, and even then, like I said about the bed, I'm still physically revved up and thrashing around. So, no, falling asleep at the wheel or nodding off at my desk? Never happens. I'm just running on this endless, exhausting supply of nervous energy all day long.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had any major changes in your health recently—like a new diagnosis, a new medication you started taking, changes to an existing medication, or any kind of surgery or illness—around the time this constant motor and restlessness started?
turns.patient_response:
Recently? Oh, gosh, no. No, nothing like that. I'm actually healthy as a horse, thankfully. I mean, I go to my general practitioner—Dr. Henderson, he's over at that clinic on Elm Street, been seeing him for probably fifteen years now—and I just had my annual physical back in the fall. He always tells me my blood pressure is fantastic for a guy my age, which is honestly a miracle considering the stress of the education system these days. I don't take any daily medications, just a standard multivitamin in the morning with my coffee, and maybe an ibuprofen if my knees are barking after a long day of chasing kids around on those hard concrete floors at school. But no new prescriptions, no surgeries, no weird viruses or anything of the sort. 

But, well, the thing about your question is... you asked if anything changed around the time this started. The thing is, Doc, this didn't just *start*. This isn't some new development that popped up out of nowhere a few months ago. I've been like this... well, forever. Literally my whole life! My poor mother, rest her soul, she used to say I was born with a lawnmower engine attached to my backside. 

I can vividly remember being in third grade—Mrs. Gable's class, she was one of those old-school, incredibly strict teachers who would practically use a metronome to keep us in line—and she actually took a roll of masking tape and made a square on the floor around my desk. She told me I wasn't allowed to step outside the tape because I was just constantly up, wandering the aisles, checking the pencil sharpener, looking out the window, you name it. And even with the tape, I'd just stand inside that little square and bounce on my toes or drum my hands on the desk until she'd threaten to send me to the principal's office. 

So, no, it's not like I hit 58 and suddenly forgot how to sit in a chair. It's been my normal for as long as I can remember. I think maybe it's just... I don't know, maybe it feels more obvious now? Or maybe my wife is just getting less tolerant of it now that our own kids are grown and moved out. When the house was full of teenagers, my pacing and constantly fixing things blended right in with the general chaos of raising a family. Now that it's just the two of us in a quiet house, I think my inability to just sit on the couch and watch a movie with her for two hours is a lot more glaring. But medically? No changes at all. Just the same old me, running at a hundred miles an hour like always.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned this has been going on your whole life since third grade. But I'm curious—in the years before recently, say five or ten years ago, were you able to manage it better, or has it always felt this intense and exhausting? And have there been any periods in your adult life where you felt like you could actually relax and sit still for an hour or two without feeling that constant motor?
turns.patient_response:
Well, see, that's the million-dollar question, isn't it? Because you're right, I've always had the motor. Always. Like I said about third grade, it's just who I am. But... was it always this *intense*? This exhausting? No. No, it wasn't. 

I used to be able to channel it a lot better, I think. If you asked me five or ten years ago, I'd say I was just a really active guy. I'd come home from school, and if I couldn't sit still, I'd just go out to the garage and tinker with the lawnmower, or I'd reorganize the basement, or I'd take the dog for a long hike. I had... I had space to let the engine run, I guess you could say. I was still moving constantly, but I was doing productive things with it, so I didn't feel this terribly wound up and drained by the end of the day. 

But this current level of trouble? This feeling like I'm just crawling out of my skin and completely exhausted by my own body? That's new. Well, relatively new. This specific level of trouble has been going on for about eight months now. 

And I know exactly why, too. About eight months ago, an older relative of ours—my wife's aunt, actually, Aunt Shirley, she's 82—she couldn't safely live on her own anymore, so she moved in with us. We put her in that guest room down the hall I was telling you about earlier. And, you know, don't get me wrong, I love Shirley, I really do. She's a sweet lady. But having her in the house has completely upended our entire ecosystem. 

She needs a lot of quiet, and she goes to bed incredibly early, like 6:30 or 7:00 in the evening. So all my usual ways of burning off this energy? Gone. I can't go down to the basement and run the table saw or hammer away at a project at 8 PM anymore because the noise echoes right up through the floorboards into her room. I can't pace the hallways because the hardwood floors creak, and she's a light sleeper, just like my wife. So after dinner, I'm basically confined to the living room armchair, and I'm supposed to just sit there and watch *Jeopardy* and *Wheel of Fortune* on low volume. 

It's like... imagine taking that lawnmower engine my mom talked about, and throwing a heavy, thick tarp over it while it's still running full blast. It's just overheating! I'm sitting in that chair, bouncing my leg, tapping my fingers, feeling the tension just build and build and build in my chest and my legs because I have nowhere to put all this physical energy. It is just draining the absolute life out of me. I've never felt this trapped by my own restlessness before. So, yeah, the constant moving has always been there, absolutely, but this unbearable, exhausting peak of it? That's strictly an eight-month development since Shirley took over the spare room and I lost my ability to just roam around my own house.

turns.doctor_question: When you're at work grading papers or doing that IEP paperwork you mentioned, do you find it hard to focus and concentrate on one task, or do you jump between tasks because you can't keep your attention on something, or is it more that you physically can't sit still even though your mind is willing to focus on the work?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, it's definitely the physical part. My mind is sharp as a tack, honestly. I don't have any trouble at all focusing on the actual words on the page or losing my train of thought. It's entirely physical. My brain is perfectly willing to do the work, but my body just flat-out refuses to stay in the chair while I do it. 

You know, those IEPs—Individualized Education Programs—they are incredibly dense documents. You've got your present levels of performance, the measurable annual goals, the accommodations, the behavioral intervention plans... it's a lot of legal jargon and data tracking. If I couldn't focus, I'd never get them done, and believe me, the school district is incredibly strict about compliance deadlines. Just last Tuesday, I had to write up a transition plan for a student—great kid, moving up to the high school next year, really needs a solid roadmap for vocational skills—and I knew exactly what I needed to write. My brain was totally dialed into the task. I wasn't getting distracted by things out the window or forgetting what I was doing. 

The problem is just that my body won't cooperate with the physical act of sitting at the desk to type it out. I'll read a paragraph of the school psychologist's evaluation, and my brain is processing the information perfectly, but my legs are just... screaming to stand up. So I'll stand up. I'll take my laptop and set it on top of the tall filing cabinet near the door and type standing up for a minute. Then I'll pace to the back of the room while I think of how to phrase a specific math goal. And the whole time I'm pacing, I am completely focused on that math goal. I'm not jumping to a different task, I'm not losing my place. I'm just literally incapable of keeping my backside glued to the swivel chair. 

It's almost like my brain and my body are operating on two completely different wavelengths. The brain says, "Okay, let's sit and knock out this paperwork," and the body says, "Great idea, but let's do a marathon while we think about it." My wife used to ask me how I could grade thirty spelling tests while walking circles around the kitchen island, but for me, that's just how it works. The moving doesn't take my attention away from the task; I just have to be in constant motion while I do it. So, no, no issues with concentration or jumping around because I'm distracted. I just can't sit still to save my life.

turns.doctor_question: Has your doctor ever checked your thyroid function, or have you ever been told you might have an overactive thyroid?
turns.patient_response:
My thyroid? You know, it's funny you ask about that, because my sister-in-law—my wife's sister, Brenda—she actually had a whole ordeal with her thyroid a few years back. I think hers was underactive? Or, wait, maybe it was overactive, because I remember she was losing weight and her heart was racing all the time, and she had to go see a specialist over at the university hospital to get it sorted out. She takes this tiny little pill for it every morning now. 

But for me? No, never. Like I was telling you earlier, I see Dr. Henderson every single fall, regular as clockwork, right before the school year really gets crazy. And he’s a fantastic doctor, incredibly thorough. He always orders the full blood workup before I come in—you know, the standard panels, cholesterol, blood sugar, all of that good stuff. When I go in for the physical, he literally prints out the results and we sit there in his office, and he goes down the list line by line with his reading glasses perched on the end of his nose. 

He's never once mentioned my thyroid being out of whack or even brought it up as a concern. If he had checked it and found something off, he absolutely would have told me, because he's a real stickler for the details. He usually just pats me on the shoulder and says, "Keep doing what you're doing, your labs are completely boring," which I guess is exactly what you want to hear from your doctor at my age! 

So, no, nobody has ever diagnosed me with an overactive thyroid or even suggested it might be the culprit. I mean, I suppose it's possible it's just never been specifically tested on those routine panels, I don't really know exactly which abbreviations stand for what on those lab sheets. But I feel like with how much I'm always moving, if it were a sudden medical condition like Brenda had, it would have shown up in my heart rate or my blood pressure or something by now, right? But no, my physical health is completely unremarkable. It's just this same restless energy I've had since I was bouncing around in Mrs. Gable's masking-tape square, long before anyone would be worrying about a 58-year-old guy's thyroid!

But let me ask you this: if you had those outlets back—if you could go down to the basement and work on projects again, or pace around freely without worrying about disturbing her—do you think you'd feel significantly better, or do you think this constant motor would still be just as intense and exhausting even with all that physical activity available to you?
turns.patient_response:
That is... gosh, that is a really good question. I actually sit there in that living room armchair and ask myself that exact same thing while the TV is humming in the background. If Shirley were to, say, move into a lovely assisted living facility tomorrow—which we've actually looked into, by the way, there's a really nice one over on Elm Street with a community garden, but they have a two-year waiting list—if she moved out and I got my house back, would I instantly feel better? 

Honestly? I don't know. I really don't know for sure. 

Because part of me thinks, yes, absolutely! If I could just go down to the basement right now... I have this whole workbench set up down there, pegboards, all my tools perfectly organized. I was in the middle of restoring this beautiful antique rocking chair before she moved in, just sanding it down by hand. If I could just go down there and sand that wood for two hours, I'd burn off the crazy energy, right? That’s how I always survived. That's how I managed the engine.

But then... then I think about how incredibly deep this exhaustion is right now. It’s practically in my bones. And I wonder, am I just getting older? I mean, I'm 58. Carrying this... this constant, revving motor inside me every single minute of every single day... maybe it's just finally catching up to me. Maybe even if I *could* pace the hallway—and it's a long hallway, beautiful original oak floors, but they squeak terribly right by the linen closet, which is why I absolutely cannot walk them at night with her sleeping—even if I could walk ten miles around my kitchen island grading my students' spelling tests again, maybe I'd still feel this wiped out just from the sheer effort of being me. 

It's sort of like a pressure cooker, you know? If you take the lid off, the water is still boiling inside. The heat is still there. The motor is still running full blast. So taking the lid off—getting my basement back, getting my pacing space back—it might stop me from feeling like I'm going to physically explode out of my skin every night, but... I just don't know if it would actually make the motor itself any less intense or any less draining at the end of the day. It's a really tough thing to untangle. I wish I had a crystal ball to tell you, I really do, because I'd love to know if there's a light at the end of this tunnel or if this heavy, exhausted feeling is just... my new normal now. I mean, in your experience, when people have this kind of energy their whole lives, does it just naturally get harder to manage as they get closer to sixty, or...?

But once you're deeply asleep—say, a few hours into the night—does that thrashing and restless movement continue throughout the whole night, or does it calm down and you sleep more peacefully once you're in deep sleep?
turns.patient_response:
Gosh, you know, that’s a really good question, but I honestly... I couldn't tell you for sure. Because, well, I'm asleep! Or at least, I assume I'm asleep. It's hard to be a reliable witness to your own unconscious habits, you know? 

You'd probably really have to ask my wife, Linda, to get a minute-by-minute breakdown of the night. Though, to be fair to her, once she finally gets to sleep, she's usually out like a light. She works over at the county library—she's the head archivist there, actually, so she spends all day on her feet hauling these heavy, dusty boxes of historical records around, which means by the time her head hits the pillow, she's absolutely exhausted. 

But as for whether the thrashing actually stops when I hit that deep sleep stage... I really have no idea. I can only tell you about the aftermath in the morning. We upgraded to a king-size bed a few years ago specifically because she said sleeping next to me was like sleeping next to a malfunctioning windmill. We even got one of those expensive memory foam mattresses, the kind where they show the commercial with the glass of wine on one side and someone jumping on the other, thinking it would absorb all my motion. And it does help a little bit, but every single morning without fail, the bed looks like a professional wrestling match took place on top of it. 

I mean, Linda loves these nice Egyptian cotton sheets, the 800-thread-count ones, and we have to buy the fitted sheets with the extra-deep pockets that are supposed to guarantee they never pop off the corners of the mattress. But almost every morning, my side of the fitted sheet is completely pulled up, the flat sheet is twisted around my legs like a tourniquet, and Linda is usually glaring at me over her morning coffee because I apparently kicked her in the calf at some point in the night. 

So I must be moving a whole awful lot. But whether that's happening right at midnight, or at 3 AM when I'm in the deepest part of my sleep, or if it's just a constant, rolling boil all night long? I really couldn't say. I just know I wake up feeling like I've been running a marathon in my dreams. I wish I could give you a better timeline of the thrashing, I really do, but I'm just completely unaware of what my body is doing once I finally manage to drift off.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a very long, excessively detailed response to a simple question, including irrelevant information about their wife's job, a mattress commercial, and the thread count of their sheets.

turns.doctor_question: When you're lying in bed at night trying to sleep, or sitting in that armchair in the evening, is the restlessness and movement you're experiencing mostly in your legs—like an urge to kick or move your legs specifically—or is it more of a full-body restlessness where your whole body just needs to move?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, no, no, it’s definitely not just my legs. I know exactly what you mean, though, because my neighbor, Tom—he lives two doors down, the guy with the absolutely immaculate lawn—he actually has that restless leg thing. He was telling me over the fence last summer that it feels like bugs crawling under his skin, and he has to literally walk around the block at two in the morning just to get his calves to settle down so he can sleep. 

But for me? No, it’s nothing like that. It’s... it’s my entire being. 

When I'm sitting in that armchair in the evenings—it's this big, overstuffed brown corduroy recliner, the kind that just sort of swallows you whole, which we’ve had for probably fifteen years. It's incredibly comfortable usually, but these days, with Shirley in the house and me not being able to go down to the basement to work it off, sitting in it feels like being strapped to a torture device. Because it’s not just my legs wanting to move. My fingers are constantly drumming on the armrests, tapping out little rhythms. My shoulders get incredibly tight. I'm constantly shifting my weight, you know, leaning to the left, then leaning to the right, adjusting the lumbar pillow, trying to stretch my back, rolling my neck... It’s like my whole body is just... humming. Humming with this trapped electricity.

If it were just my legs, I almost think that would be a relief! I could just bounce my knee, which I do anyway, obviously. I mean, I'm sure you've noticed my knee has been bouncing under this desk basically since I sat down in your office. But at night, when I'm trying to force myself to relax and watch Jeopardy with Linda and Aunt Shirley... it’s my arms, it’s my chest, it's this overwhelming, full-body sensation that I need to get up and do something, *anything*. 

It's that motor I keep talking about. It doesn't just power the wheels, it powers the whole chassis, you know? It’s completely systemic. So, yeah, definitely a full-body experience. It's just... it's exhausting trying to keep the whole machine in park when the engine is revving that high, and every single part of the car is vibrating because of it.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes drumming his fingers, constantly shifting his weight in his seat, and bouncing his knee.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an overwhelming, full-body sensation of restlessness and a strong urge to get up and do something.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly compares his constant internal drive to being powered by a motor with an engine that is revving high.

turns.doctor_question: When you're sitting in that armchair at night and you feel the urge to move your legs, do you experience any uncomfortable sensations in your legs themselves—like tingling, crawling, burning, aching, or a sensation like something is moving under the skin—or is it purely a physical urge to move without any of those uncomfortable feelings?
turns.patient_response:
Well, no, it’s really just exactly like I was saying before—it's that pure, unadulterated urge to just... go. There’s absolutely no pain or weird sensations in the skin or the muscles themselves. 

Like I mentioned with my neighbor Tom and his whole "bugs under the skin" thing, I don't get anything even remotely close to that. No tingling, no crawling, no burning. It’s not an ache, either. I mean, I know what an ache feels like! I teach special ed in one of those modular portable classrooms out behind the main middle school building, and they just slapped this incredibly thin, cheap industrial carpet directly over a concrete slab. So after seven or eight hours of pacing around that room, redirecting kids and bending over their desks to help with math worksheets, my arches and my calves will legitimately ache from the concrete. I know that feeling well. 

But what happens in the armchair at night is completely different. It’s not uncomfortable in a... in a sensory way, if that makes sense? I don't feel anything moving under my skin. It’s purely just this massive, undeniable physical command from my brain saying, "We need to move. Right now." 

It feels more like a coiled spring. You know when you wind up one of those little toy cars, the ones you pull back on the floor, and you can feel the tension in the gears just begging you to let go so it can shoot across the room? That’s what my legs feel like. That's what my whole body feels like, really. There's no burning, no numbness. If I try to ignore it and just force myself to sit there and watch the television, my legs don't start hurting or tingling... the urge just gets louder and louder and more impossible to ignore until I'm practically jumping out of the corduroy cushions. So, yeah, no weird nerve feelings or anything like that. Just... just a totally restless engine that's stuck in drive while my foot is slamming on the brake.

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an intense, undeniable physical urge to move and feeling like a 'coiled spring', indicating severe internal restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly describes feeling like a 'restless engine that's stuck in drive', which directly matches the symptom of acting as if 'driven by a motor'.

turns.doctor_question: Has your wife ever mentioned that your leg movements at night follow a pattern—like, does she notice your legs kicking in a rhythmic, repetitive way, almost like you're pedaling a bicycle over and over, or is it more just random thrashing and shifting around?
turns.patient_response:
A bicycle? Oh, gosh, no, nothing as organized as that. I mean, if I were pedaling a bicycle in my sleep, Linda would probably be absolutely thrilled because at least it would be predictable, right? She could just, you know, stay out of the bike lane, so to speak! But no, she’s never mentioned anything about a rhythm or a pattern. It’s completely random. 

Actually, I remember one morning—this was probably a couple of months ago, right before Shirley moved in and our whole routine got thrown out the window—Linda was sitting at the kitchen island with her coffee, just looking at me with these dark circles under her eyes, and she said, "You were doing the spastic starfish again last night." That’s what she calls it! The spastic starfish. Because it’s just an arm flying out this way, a leg shooting out that way, flipping from my back to my stomach, then rolling over and taking all those expensive Egyptian cotton sheets with me. 

There’s absolutely no rhythm to it. It’s not like a steady, repetitive kicking where she can just time it and dodge. It’s more like... well, it’s like a fish flopping on a dock. Just sudden, explosive movements out of nowhere. I might lay completely still for ten minutes—or at least she thinks I am—and then suddenly I’m launching my knee into the center of the mattress or throwing my arm over my head. 

Sometimes she even tries to build this little barricade of pillows between us, just to absorb the shock of whatever random limb comes flying her way. So, no, definitely not a pedaling motion or anything rhythmic. Just total, unpredictable chaos all night long. I really do feel terrible about it, because like I said, she works so hard hauling those heavy boxes at the archives and she desperately needs her rest, but it's just completely random thrashing. I have zero control over it once I'm out.

turns.doctor_question: When you're lying in bed and you feel that urge to move your legs, if you really tried hard to keep your legs completely still for, say, five or ten minutes, do you think you could hold them still if you concentrated on it, or is it physically impossible to resist the urge no matter how hard you try?
turns.patient_response:
Five or ten minutes? Gosh, I... I honestly don't know if I could give you a straight answer on that. I'm really not sure, because I don't think I've ever actually made it that long to find out if it's strictly, you know, physically impossible. 

I mean, I *do* try. Believe me, I try so hard, especially lately. With Aunt Shirley's oxygen machine humming down the hall and the whole house just feeling so tense, I know Linda desperately needs uninterrupted sleep. So I'll lie there flat on my back, staring up at the ceiling fan—we have this one blade that's slightly warped, so it wobbles and makes this tiny ticking sound on medium speed—and I will just focus every single ounce of my willpower on my legs. I'll tell myself, "Don't move. Do not move a muscle." 

And for the first minute, maybe a minute and a half? I think I'm doing it. I'm holding the line. But the amount of concentration it takes is just... it's astronomical. It’s exactly like trying to hold your breath underwater. You know you can do it for a little bit, but eventually, your lungs start burning, your brain starts screaming at you that you need air, and the panic just builds and builds. Except for me, it’s not my lungs, it’s that coiled spring feeling I was talking about. It just gets tighter and tighter the longer I try to force it to stay still. 

So, is it physically impossible to resist? I really couldn't say. I don't know if my body would literally force a movement if I somehow managed to keep my brain locked in on it, or if my brain just gives up first because the urge gets so incredibly loud and overwhelming. Usually, what happens is I'm focusing so intensely on freezing my legs that the energy just leaks out somewhere else—I'll suddenly realize my jaw is completely clenched, or my fingers are gripping the bedsheets like I'm hanging off a cliff, and then I just... snap. The dam breaks, and I have to roll over or kick my leg out just to release all that built-up pressure. 

Ten minutes just feels like an absolute eternity when you're lying in the dark fighting your own chassis like that. So, yeah, I've never really timed it, and I don't know if it's a true impossibility. I just know I haven't been able to win that staring contest with my own body yet.

turns.doctor_question: Before your wife's aunt moved in eight months ago, when you had complete freedom to move around your basement and hallways whenever you wanted—say, back when you were working on that antique rocking chair—did you still feel that same constant motor running inside you at night when you were trying to sleep, or did having that outlet during the day actually help you feel calmer and more settled once you got into bed?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, well... no, having the basement to myself didn't make the motor stop. I mean, sure, it was absolutely wonderful having that space. When I was restoring that antique rocking chair—it was a really beautiful piece, solid oak, probably early 1900s, and I spent hours down there just sanding it, staining it, pacing around the workbench and working off some of that physical energy. But when I actually went upstairs and got into bed? The engine was still idling high. It always has been. 

Because, see, this isn't some new development just because Aunt Shirley moved in and hijacked the guest room and turned the hallway into an obstacle course. This is... this is just who I am. It's been a part of who I was long before adulthood, long before I ever met Linda or bought this house. This definitely isn't something that just started with this recent family change. 

In fact, my mother, God rest her soul, she used to always joke about it. She’d tell everyone at family gatherings that even back in elementary school, I practically taught the class from my seat. Or, well, I guess not *from* my seat, because the whole punchline was that I was *always* out of my chair. Constantly. Just wandering the aisles, looking at what the other kids were doing, or I'd be talking non-stop to whoever was unlucky enough to be sitting next to me. 

And the interrupting—oh, I was terrible about cutting in before the teacher even finished giving directions. Like, Mrs. Gable in third grade would be halfway through explaining a spelling worksheet, and I’d just blurt out the answer or ask what we were supposed to do next before she could even take a breath. My brain was just always ten steps ahead, and my body was right there with it, just completely unable to wait its turn. 

So, yeah, having the basement was a nice outlet, and losing it has definitely made things feel more... confined, I guess? Especially with all the oxygen tubes and boxes everywhere now. But that constant motor running inside me at night? That didn't just start eight months ago. That engine has been running on full throttle since I was a little kid in short pants. It's just always been there, buzzing away, whether I had a basement to pace around in or not.

turns.doctor_question: When you're lying in bed at night and you get that urge to move your legs, let me ask you this very specifically: Is there any uncomfortable feeling happening *in* your legs themselves—like a restlessness or tension that feels like it's coming from inside the leg muscles or under the skin—that makes you feel like you *have* to move them to make that uncomfortable feeling go away? Or is it purely a mental urge to move without any actual discomfort in the legs themselves?
turns.patient_response:
Uncomfortable feeling in the legs... like under the skin? No, gosh no. I know exactly what you mean, though, or at least I think I do. One of the paraprofessionals I work with at the school—I'm a special education teacher, by the way, mostly working with the older kids, which is a whole lot of pacing and standing and redirecting all day long—but anyway, she has that thing where she says it feels like literal bugs are crawling through her veins at night, and she has to get up and do deep lunges just to make it stop hurting. 

But for me? No, absolutely nothing like that. My legs themselves feel perfectly fine. I mean, sure, they might be a little tired from standing in a classroom all day or chasing down a runaway teenager in the cafeteria, but there's no actual physical discomfort in the muscles or the joints. There's no tingling, no burning, no creepy-crawly feeling under the skin that I'm trying to scratch by moving. 

It is entirely, one hundred percent, just a mental urge. Well, I say mental, but it's like... it's like my brain is just stuck in drive, and my legs are just the wheels that happen to be attached to the engine. The engine is humming, so the wheels just want to spin. It’s not that my calf is aching and a kick will make the ache go away. It’s just that my brain is screaming, "We are awake! We have energy! We should be doing something!" And since I'm lying flat on my back in the dark, kicking a leg out or flipping over is the only "something" my body can manage to do. 

So, no, if you were to somehow disconnect my brain from my legs, the legs themselves wouldn't be complaining at all. They're not uncomfortable. It's just that constant, buzzing need to be in motion that comes from somewhere else entirely. I just... I just have to move. I don't know if that makes total sense, but yeah, no weird physical sensations in the legs themselves whatsoever.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes kicking a leg out or flipping over in bed as a physical manifestation of their need to move.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes a constant, buzzing mental urge and a feeling that they 'just have to move,' indicating internal restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly uses a motor metaphor to describe their energy, stating their brain is 'stuck in drive' and the 'engine is humming.'
